title: How Motion Detection Zones Work and Why You Should Set Them
excerpt: Motion zones let a camera ignore swaying trees and passing headlights while still catching real movement. Learn how zones work, then draw, place, and test them.
author: HiddenCameras Editorial Team
authorBio: The HiddenCameras.tv editorial team researches and writes about security cameras, surveillance technology, and home safety.
body:
A motion detection zone is a shape you draw over your camera's live view and tell it: only react to movement in here. Everything outside the shape is ignored, permanently. Done right, zones turn a camera that fires at every leaf into one that fires when it actually matters.

What the camera is really detecting

Most app-based zones work on pixel changes: the camera compares each frame to the last, and when enough pixels inside your zone change beyond a threshold, it triggers recording and alerts. That is why a drawn square on a screen has any power at all — the camera is watching a subset of the image, not the world.

PIR-only cameras cannot draw zones

Passive infrared (PIR) sensors detect heat movement, not pixels, so they have no zones to draw. Many cameras pair a PIR wake-up with pixel analysis to confirm, which is why their apps still offer zones. If your camera is PIR-only, sensitivity and physical placement are your only controls.

Draw the zone in ten minutes

  1. Open the live view in the camera's app and find the detection or zone settings.
  2. Draw the zone over the area that matters: a doormat, a driveway, a gate.
  3. Exclude everything else: street, trees, sky, the neighbor's fence line.
  4. Set sensitivity to the middle, then adjust after real-world testing.
  5. Save and walk the approach yourself to confirm the alert fires.

Why zones cut false alerts

Every false alert is movement outside your goal area: headlights sweeping a fence, a branch at the frame edge, rain streaking the lens. Zones remove those triggers by removing them from the detection field. Two false-alert sources zones cannot fix: insects crawling directly on the lens, which register as huge close-up motion, and low sun washing the whole frame. Wipe the lens and drop sensitivity for those. If alerts spike after a storm, check whether wind moved the camera itself; a shifted mount redraws every zone boundary without telling you.

Zone shapes for three common goals

Package delivery: a small rectangle on the doormat

Tight zones around the drop point mean a carrier placing a box triggers an alert, and so does anyone who approaches it afterward. Include the carrier's first step onto the porch so you capture the approach, not just the handoff.

Driveway: a long strip, excluding the road

Draw a strip along the driveway and cut the street out of the frame, or every passing car becomes an event. Keep the garage exit inside the strip so departures are recorded.

Pet area: decide whether you want pet alerts

If you want to know when a pet reaches a room, the pet's corridor stays inside the zone. If pets already generate too many alerts, redraw the zone above pet height — a counter-level zone catches people, not cats.

Stack person alerts on top of zones

Zones control where the camera looks; person, vehicle, and pet filters control what it reports. Running both at once is how a busy porch stops buzzing: the zone narrows the field to the doormat and walkway, and the person filter drops the remaining non-human motion inside that field, like a ball rolling across the steps. Either layer alone still over-alerts; together they cut noise dramatically.

Order matters when you tune them. Draw and test the zone first with all filters off, so you know the raw detection field works. Then switch the person filter on and repeat the walk test, including the edge cases your household produces: a crouching courier, a child, someone carrying a large box that hides their torso. If the filter drops real events, widen the zone slightly or raise sensitivity one notch before blaming the filter. Finish by re-testing at night, because filters trained mostly on daylight footage miss more after dark.

Test like a thief, not a homeowner

Walk your real approach at night, with a box, from the street. Confirm the alert arrives fast enough to show a face, then check the stored clip. Re-test after seasons change, because growing trees and shifting sun can turn a good zone into a false-alert machine.
